skill.displayName: 波龙股神量化交易系统

vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: bowlong-quant-aio
Version: 2.1.2

The bundle is a comprehensive and well-structured quantitative trading toolkit for the Chinese A-share and futures markets. It includes modules for stock selection, backtesting, and real-time risk monitoring, with support for local trading terminals like Huaxin QMT and Wenhua WH8. While the system handles sensitive information such as API tokens (Tushare) and trading credentials, the code (e.g., scripts/executor_huaxin.py and scripts/risk_monitor.py) uses these secrets only for their intended purposes—communicating with official financial APIs, local trading services (127.0.0.1), or the official Telegram API for notifications. No evidence of data exfiltration, malicious execution, or prompt injection was found.

llm.summary: The skill's code and instructions match a quantitative trading system, but there are inconsistencies in declared requirements and it asks for sensitive trading credentials and can place orders — treat as high-risk and review carefully before supplying secrets or enabling autonomous use.

dimensions.detail: The code files (stock picker, backtester, QMT/WH8 executors, risk monitor) clearly implement the claimed quant-trading features (selection, backtest, execution, risk alerts). Asking for market-data tokens (Tushare) and broker credentials (QMT/WH8/TBQuant) is coherent with the stated purpose. However, registry metadata earlier reported no required env vars while the SKILL.md and code require TUSHARE_TOKEN and many broker credentials — this mismatch should be resolved.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: Runtime instructions tell the agent to run local Python scripts that read config files, connect to broker APIs (local HTTP or COM), and can send alerts to external services (Telegram). Those actions are within the skill's purpose but they involve reading credentials, connecting to local services (127.0.0.1 ports) and making network calls to place/cancel orders. There is no unexpected exfiltration endpoint in the docs, but the scripts have the ability to perform high-impact operations (real trading) if real credentials/mode=live are used.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec; the skill is instruction/code-only and only recommends pip installs for common Python libraries. No downloaded archives or third‑party installer URLs were bundled, which reduces supply-chain risk.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The SKILL.md and config files reference sensitive environment variables (TUSHARE_TOKEN, QMT_ACCOUNT, QMT_PASSWORD, WH8_ACCOUNT, WH8_PASSWORD, TB_ACCOUNT, TB_PASSWORD, PUSH_TOKEN, PUSH_CHAT_ID). Requiring broker account credentials and push tokens is consistent with full functionality but is high-privilege. Also there is an inconsistency: registry metadata claimed no required env vars while SKILL.md lists TUSHARE_TOKEN and many config files reference additional secrets that are not declared centrally — that incomplete declaration is a red flag.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill is not marked always:true, but it contains code that can perform autonomous actions (place/cancel orders) when run and the platform default allows autonomous invocation. Combined with access to broker credentials, this raises the blast radius: an agent invoking the skill (or a user running the scripts) could execute real trades if configured in live mode. The skill writes/reads its own config files but does not appear to modify other skills.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This package appears to be a real quantitative trading toolkit and includes executors that can connect to broker APIs and Telegram. Before installing or providing secrets: 1) Resolve the metadata mismatch — confirm which env vars are actually required. 2) Do not supply real broker credentials until you have audited the executor code and tested thoroughly in paper/simulated mode. 3) If you must test, set executor mode to paper and run on an isolated machine or sandbox with no access to production accounts. 4) Consider restricting network access (e.g., prevent outbound HTTP except to trusted endpoints) while you review. 5) Review scripts that issue requests (executor_*.py, risk_monitor.py) to ensure no unexpected remote endpoints or hardcoded URLs. 6) If you plan to let the agent call this skill autonomously, accept that it could place trades when configured live; limit or avoid granting real credentials in that scenario. If you want, I can: (a) list all places in the code that read environment variables or send network requests, (b) show exactly which lines call external services, or (c) extract the minimal subset of files needed for offline backtesting only.
